India finished the 2026 Commonwealth Games with 39 medals to its name - 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze. It placed India in fourth place behind Australia, England and Canada. Boxing and athletics produced the most medals (10) with weightlifting (8) and para-athletics (6) next in the order.In the truncated quadrennial event, held without shooting, wrestling, badminton, table tennis and field hockey, all of which have contributed significantly to India's coffers in the past, the country finished with 22 medals fewer than the 2022 edition in Birmingham (61 medals).Gulveer Singh emerged as the only multiple medallist for India at the Games. His silver in 10,000m and bronze in 5,000m made him the first Indian track and field athlete to win two individual medals at a single CWG edition.The Aligarh-born Naib Subedar made his international breakthrough with a bronze medal in the 5000m at the 2023 Asian Athletics Championships and followed it up with another third-place finish at the rescheduled 2022 Asian Games.The 28-year-old national record holder in 5000m, 10,000m, one mile and half-marathon trains regularly at the high-performance centre in Colorado Springs, USA, where steps towards his multiple feats and medals are forged.A Target Olympic Podium Scheme (TOPS) athlete, he's been assisted with Rs 30.40 lakh during this CWG cycle and Rs 25.32 lakh under the Annual Calendar for Training and Competition (ACTC).Behind every medal is days and weeks of training and preparation backed by government and funding by private players.Before the Glasgow Games got underway, the track and field athletes and para-athletes underwent training at the Spala Olympic Training Centre in Poland; boxers spent time in Belfast; the lifters travelled to Birmingham while the Artistic Gymnastics team set camp in South Essex.All such tours were sponsored by the government through its ACTC fund and TOPS.TOPS, a division formed in September 2014, operates as the Sports Ministry's flagship programme to support India's athletes win medals at the Olympics. It is presently headed by Col. Nachhatar Singh Johal, who represented the country in sailing at the 2008 Beijing Olympics.Earlier this year, TOPS' ambit increased to 27 sports with six getting priority: archery, badminton, boxing, hockey, shooting and wrestling.Subsequently, Target Asian Games Group (TAGG), which was created last year to provide support to select athletes was disbanded this year. It had begun with an initial pool of 16 disciplines and 37 athletes.However, its responsibilities will now be shared between TOPS and Training of Elite Athletes and Management Support (TEAMS) divisions. TOPS and TEAMS will manage day-to-day operations, development, and coordination for 27 specific disciplines.TOPS selects athletes based on their medal potential rather than a single qualifying criterion. The scheme assesses recent international performances, world rankings, consistency at the elite level, long-term progression and potential to win medals at the Olympics and other major events. Recommendations from the Mission Olympic Cell (MOC), National Sports Federations (NSFs), coaches, foreign experts and sports science teams also play a key role.Athletes are divided into two categories:Core Group: Established athletes with immediate medal prospects.Development Group: Emerging athletes being prepared for future Olympic cycles.Their performances are monitored regularly to ensure support matches their progress.There is no fixed annual funding cap under TOPS. Instead, assistance is tailored to each athlete's requirements, depending on their sport, training programme and competition calendar.Funding can cover:For athletes in high-performance Olympic and Paralympic disciplines requiring overseas training and advanced support systems, annual funding can run into several lakhs or even crores of rupees. Every proposal undergoes technical and financial scrutiny before approval by the MOC.TOPS follows a two-pronged approach—backing athletes capable of winning medals immediately while simultaneously investing in future prospects.This is achieved through:The objective is to maximise India's medal chances today while creating a pipeline of athletes for future Olympic, Asian Games, Commonwealth Games and Paralympic cycles.Athletes are monitored continuously, with periodic reviews conducted by the Mission Olympic Cell alongside NSFs, coaches and technical experts.Reviews consider:TOPS follows a performance-linked funding model. If an athlete consistently underperforms, remains inactive without valid reasons or repeatedly misses agreed benchmarks, financial support can be reduced or withdrawn after evaluation.However, genuine circumstances such as injuries, rehabilitation or long-term planning are also taken into account before any decision is made.Yes. TOPS has expanded beyond traditional funding to provide a comprehensive high-performance support system.Support can include:The aim is to give Indian athletes access to the same integrated support systems available in leading sporting nations, with greater emphasis on recovery, injury management, mental resilience and scientific preparation.TOPS says its funding decisions are guided by transparency, accountability and merit. Every proposal passes through multiple stages of evaluation involving NSFs, coaches, sports science experts, the MOC and financial scrutiny under government procedures.Funding decisions are based on measurable criteria, including:The scheme also incorporates periodic reviews, stakeholder consultations, documented approval processes and audit mechanisms to ensure public funds are used effectively. Its stated vision is that no Indian athlete with genuine medal potential should miss out on world-class preparation because of financial constraints.It is now 10 years to the 2036 Olympics, a Summer Games that India intends to host in Ahmedabad. If awarded, the goal there will not just be showcase its culture and ability to host an event of such scale but to compete with the best. To that end, the Union Cabinet has approved a revamped Khelo India Scheme and enhanced assistance to National Sports Federations (NSFs).For the period of 2026-27 to 2030-31, which covers the 2030 CWG, LA 2028, Brisbane 2032 and five years leading to the 2036 Summer Games, a combined outlay of Rs 36,441 crore has been planned - Rs 29,054 crore towards Khelo India Scheme and Rs 7,387 crore to the NSFs.The revamped, and enhanced, Khelo India Scheme is nearly eight times the previous budget allocation (Rs 2532.22 crore from 2021-2026) towards grassroots development.After the positive returns at the Commonwealth Games, a tougher test awaits the Indian contingent later in the year at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan from September 19. And then further down the line at the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles, the necessary off-the-field steps for which have already been taken.
Article Summary: Neeraj Chopra won the silver medal in the men's javelin throw final at the Commonwealth Games 2026, in Glasgow, Scotland. Chopra will compete for India at the 2016 Olympics in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. He will be competing for India in the 4x100m and 4x400m relay events.

Article Title: 'A coterie hijacked him': Report claims Pakistan federation distanced itself from Arshad Nadeem before CWG flop
Article Text:
Pakistan's Arshad Nadeem (PTI Photo)

Federation 'distanced itself' from Olympic champion's preparations

Coach admits Nadeem was underprepared

Pakistan sporting structure under scrutiny

'A coterie hijacked him': Mentors question Nadeem's preparation

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Pakistan's Olympic champion Arshad Nadeem has found himself at the centre of growing criticism following his disappointing Commonwealth Games campaign in Glasgow, with questions now being raised not just about his form but also about the support system that surrounded him in the lead-up to the competition.The defending Commonwealth Games champion endured one of the worst outings of his career, finishing ninth after failing to produce a throw beyond 80 metres. Sri Lanka's Rumesh Pathirage clinched the gold medal, while India's Neeraj Chopra and Yashvir Singh completed a historic South Asian podium with silver and bronze respectively.But as scrutiny intensified over Nadeem's performance, reports from Pakistan suggested the Olympic champion had effectively been left to prepare on his own after the Pakistan Amateur Athletics Federation (PAAF) allegedly distanced itself from his training programme following a dispute over the retention of his long-time coach Salman Butt According to a PTI report, the PAAF largely withdrew support from the star javelin thrower after disagreements emerged last year over his coaching setup. The report claimed that several requests made by Nadeem regarding his training programme were not entertained, while the Pakistan Sports Board also did not release funds to facilitate foreign coaches or trainers.Instead of training overseas under renowned South African coach Terseus Liebenberg, who had guided him before his Olympic triumph, Nadeem spent his Commonwealth Games build-up in Lahore with Salman Butt and local trainers.The contrast with India's preparation was striking. While Neeraj Chopra completed his final rehabilitation and training block in Biel, Switzerland, fellow Indian javelin throwers Yashvir Singh and Rohit Yadav trained in Spala, Poland, alongside foreign coaches and support staff before heading to Glasgow.The differing approaches were reflected in the final standings as India secured two medals, while Nadeem failed to qualify among the top eight after the opening three rounds.Nadeem had arrived in Glasgow with limited competitive exposure, having competed in only one preparatory meet in Switzerland during 2026. He also trained almost exclusively in Lahore despite the vastly different weather conditions between Pakistan and Scotland.His long-time coach Salman Butt admitted the Olympic champion was far from his best and acknowledged he was underprepared for the Games.Former Pakistan Athletics Federation president Akram Sahi also blamed negligence and inadequate preparation for the dramatic decline."Since Nadeem's Olympic gold medal a coterie has hijacked him and never let him come to me," Sahi told Telecom Asia Sport."This result in Glasgow is hugely disappointing... the signs were imminent for the last several months as there was negligence and lack of training."Another mentor, speaking anonymously, argued that Nadeem had become complacent and failed to invest sufficiently in elite overseas training after receiving substantial financial rewards following his Olympic success.Nadeem's disappointing campaign has reignited debate over Pakistan's sporting ecosystem.Former Olympic boxing bronze medallist Hussain Shah described the situation as a reflection of systemic shortcomings."This is an athlete who is self-made and comes from a village and belongs to a low-income family. But he brought so much glory to Pakistan with his gold medals. And yet he couldn't prepare properly for the CWG. It is a sad reflection on our sports structure," Shah said.Pakistan's campaign in Glasgow also exposed wider concerns. Boxer Fatima Zehra, who secured the country's only medal with bronze, also lamented the lack of quality preparation and international exposure, saying better training could have helped her challenge for gold.The criticism did not stop with Pakistan's athletics authorities. Two of Nadeem's former mentors also questioned the Olympic champion's preparation, alleging that a lack of quality training and poor decisions contributed to his disappointing campaign.Akram Sahi, the former Pakistan Athletics Federation president who helped identify Nadeem's talent in 2018, claimed the warning signs had been visible for months."Since Nadeem's Olympic gold medal a coterie has hijacked him and never let him come to me," Sahi told Telecom Asia Sport."This result in Glasgow is hugely disappointing for someone who has risen to new heights, but the signs were imminent for the last several months as there was negligence and lack of training."Another mentor, speaking anonymously, echoed those concerns, suggesting Nadeem had not trained adequately after returning from Haj and had become overly dependent on official support."He won the Olympics after he got extensive training from his South African coach Terseus Liebenberg. His training stints at Northwest University Potchefstroom also helped him clinch Olympic gold. Now he waited for the federation and government to send him to South Africa for training.He should have invested in himself rather than waiting for someone else," the mentor said.The mentor also questioned Nadeem's current coaching setup, claiming his long-time coach Salman Butt lacked specialist expertise in javelin and that the Olympic champion had become distracted by business ventures after receiving substantial financial rewards following his Paris triumph.
Article Summary: Pakistan's Olympic champion Arshad Nadeem finished ninth in the javelin throw at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Reports suggest the Pakistan Amateur Athletics Federation (PAAF) 'distanced itself' from his training programme following a dispute over the retention of his long-time coach Salman Butt. Former Pakistan Athletics Federation president Akram Sahi blamed negligence and inadequate preparation for the dramatic decline. Former Olympic boxing bronze medallist Hussain Shah described the situation as a reflection of systemic shortcomings.

Article Title: CWG 2026: Relay flop raises Asian Games alarm
Article Text:
Vishal TK (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

BENGALURU: Even as India celebrated a strong athletics campaign at the Commonwealth Games — highlighted by three para athletics gold medals to go with five silver and five bronze from the able-bodied contingent — attention has now shifted to the disappointing performance of the mixed 4x400m relay team.The quartet, which made the cut after surviving a rigorous selection process that saw the Athletics Federation of India (AFI) reject all the other relay combinations, failed to deliver on the biggest stage.Vishal TK, who set a national record this season with a personal best of 44.98 seconds in May, clocked a below-par 46.1 in the opening lap in the final. Ansa Babu then struggled to match the quality of the field, clocking 54.1 while rivals, led by Jamaica’s Leah Anderson (50.8 seconds), comfortably ran under 52 seconds.Santosh Kumar Tamilarasan (46.4 seconds) and Rashdeep Kaur (53.72 seconds) were unable to change the complexion of the race as India finished sixth and last in the final rankings after Australia was disqualified and Zambia failed to finish.“It seems India’s top runners peaked too early this season. Rajesh ran 45.26 in March but his performance dipped in Glasgow. Rajesh is one of our key relay runners and, with Mohammed Anas and Amoj Jacob still recovering from injuries, he is now the most experienced member of the squad.It will take a miracle for our relay runners to improve enough before the Asian Games next month,” another coach said.Rajesh, who clocked 47.00 seconds in the heats, was replaced by Santosh for the final. Several coaches who monitored the team’s preparations also questioned whether the expertise of foreign coach Jason Alexander Dawson was being fully utilised.“Two coaches training two separate groups of athletes simply doesn’t work. Whoever can’t cope with Jason’s workload shifts to the Indian coach. Ideally, all the 400m runners should train under one programme and one brain,” one coach said, referring to the parallel coaching setup under Dawson and Raj Mohan in Thiruvananthapuram.A former national coach, who had previously handled the relay squad, urged patience. “You can’t call Vishal a sub-45 runner unless he consistently runs below 45 seconds. I’m optimistic our relay squads will bounce back and perform well at the Asian Games. Earlier, India was stronger in the women’s 4x400m relay, but now the men’s team has become more competitive,” he said.Meanwhile, AFI has reportedly decided not to field the men’s 4x100m relay team at the Asian Games while clearing the remaining relay squads.
Article Summary: The mixed 4x400m relay team failed to deliver on the biggest stage. Vishal TK, who set a national record this season with a personal best of 44.98 seconds in May, clocked a below-par 46.1 in the opening lap in the final. Ansa Babu then struggled to match the quality of the field, clocking 54.1.

Article Title: Forging champions in Olive Green: How the Army Sports Institute has become India’s premier high performance centre
Article Text:
Ankush Panghal, Jaismine Lamboria, Arundhati Choudhary and Jadumani Singh Mandengbam (Image credit: Agencies)

Building Champions, Not Just Athletes

Boxing: The Crown Jewel

The High Performance Advantage

Beyond Boxing

A Model for India’s Olympic Ambitions

NEW DELHI: The resounding success of Indian Army athletes at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow is far more than a medal-winning campaign—it is the culmination of years of scientific planning, relentless discipline and institutional excellence. At the heart of this success stands the Army Sports Institute (ASI), Pune, India’s premier military high performance centre, which has once again demonstrated why it is regarded as one of the country’s finest centres for elite athlete development.With Army boxers contributing an extraordinary haul of 8 medals at the CWG, ASI’s contribution to Indian boxing has reached unprecedented heights. From Olympic hopefuls to Commonwealth champions, the institute continues to produce athletes capable of competing—and winning—against the very best in the world.Established in 2005, the Army Sports Institute was envisioned as the Indian Army ’s flagship project to identify, nurture and develop sporting excellence. Twenty-five years later, that vision has evolved into one of the country’s most successful high-performance ecosystems.Unlike conventional training centres, ASI integrates every aspect of athlete development under one roof. Elite coaching, sports science, strength and conditioning, biomechanics, nutrition, psychology, physiotherapy, recovery management and performance analytics operate seamlessly to maximise every athlete’s potential.This holistic approach has transformed ASI into a benchmark for high-performance sport in India.Boxing has emerged as one of ASI’s greatest success stories.The institute’s talent identification programme scouts promising youngsters from across India and systematically develops them through the Boys and Girls Sports Companies before transitioning the best performers into elite national-level competitors.The results are unmistakable.At Glasgow 2026, Army boxers dominated the competition, winning medals across multiple weight categories and forming the backbone of India’s historic boxing campaign. Their performances reflected exceptional technical preparation, tactical maturity and the mental resilience that are hallmarks of Army training. India’s boxing team produced its best-ever CWG performance with seven gold and three silver medals overall, underscoring the depth of the programme.Success at ASI is not accidental.Every training session is data-driven. Athlete workloads are scientifically monitored. Recovery protocols minimise injury risk. Nutrition plans are customised. Performance is analysed through modern sports science and technology.This integrated approach ensures that athletes peak when it matters most—at international championships.Equally important is the military ethos that defines every athlete trained at ASI: discipline, resilience, teamwork and the determination to perform under pressure.While boxing has become a flagship discipline, ASI’s excellence extends across athletics, wrestling, weightlifting, diving, fencing, archery and several Olympic sports.While boxing led the Army Sports Institute’s remarkable CWG campaign, its excellence extended well beyond the ring. Army athletes scripted history in athletics with a series of landmark performances. Naib Subedar Gulveer Singh became the first Indian ever to win a silver medal in the men’s 10,000m and followed it with a historic bronze in the 5,000m—the first medal by an Indian in the event at the Commonwealth Games. In doing so, he also became the first Indian track and field athlete to win two medals at a single CWG.Adding to the historic achievements, Naib Subedar Sarvesh Kushare won the silver medal in High Jump, marking India’s first-ever CWG medal in the men’s high jump. In the weightlifting arena Hav Ajaya Babu won a silver medal and created a new record in Snatch category. Together, these breakthrough performances reaffirm that the Army Sports Institute is not merely producing champions in one discipline but is emerging as India’s most successful multi-sport high-performance centre, consistently delivering athletes capable of rewriting the nation’s sporting history.The institute has consistently produced Olympians, Asian Games medallists, CWG champions and national record holders. Many of India’s finest sporting achievements over the past decade have carried the unmistakable imprint of the Army Sports Institute.As India intensifies its preparations for future Olympic Games, the Army Sports Institute provides a proven blueprint for sustained international success.Its combination of early talent identification, world-class coaching, cutting-edge sports science and unwavering institutional support has created a system capable of producing champions year after year.The Glasgow CWG have once again reaffirmed an enduring truth: when India celebrates sporting excellence, the Army Sports Institute is often at the heart of that success.From nurturing young talent to producing Commonwealth champions, ASI continues to live its motto—transforming potential into podium finishes and inspiring a new generation of athletes to wear the Tricolour with pride.The remarkable contribution of Army athletes at Glasgow is not merely a medal tally; it is a testament to twenty-five years of vision, investment and unwavering commitment to sporting excellence. Champions are not born overnight—they are forged in Olive Green.
Article Summary: Army Sports Institute, Pune, is India’s premier military high performance centre. Boxers dominated the competition at Glasgow 2026, winning medals across multiple weight categories. Army athletes scripted history in athletics with a series of landmark performances. Naib Subedar Gulveer Singh became the first Indian ever to win a silver medal in the 10,000m.

Article Title: CWG para champions complain against IOA staff, seek action over alleged 'misconduct, disrespectful behaviour'
Article Text:
Dilip Mahadu Gavit and Mohammed Basil Morssinganakathi. (PTI Photo)

NEW DELHI: Fresh from scripting history at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, India’s men’s T47 100m gold and silver medallists Dilip Mahadu Gavit and Mohammed Basil Morssinganakathi have lodged formal complaints with the sports ministry and the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) against an IOA media committee member, alleging rude and disrespectful behaviour towards the country’s para athletes.The complaints have been filed separately by Gavit, Basil and para athletics coach Pushpa NP, who was part of the Indian contingent in Glasgow. It is learnt that Paralympic Committee of India (PCI) CEO Rahul Swami has also submitted a similar complaint to the ministry and the IOA.According to sources, the complaints name Sarvesh Kedia, an IOA media committee member who travelled to Glasgow as one of the Indian contingent’s press attaches and was attached to the chef-de-mission’s office. Kedia was among the 14 IOA officials accompanying India’s combined able-bodied and para athletes’ contingent.In a complaint accessed by TOI, Pushpa alleged that Kedia “was talking loudly with our medal winners Dilip Gavit and Basil and coaches” and said the incident involved him and chief para athletics coach Satyanarayana. She urged the authorities to ensure that Kedia “is not involved in any para athletics media interaction” in future and sought appropriate action against him.The alleged incident took place on July 30 after Gavit clocked 10.71 seconds — a Games record — to become India’s first male para athlete to win a Commonwealth Games athletics gold medal. Basil followed with a season-best of 10.83 seconds to claim silver as India completed a historic 1-2 finish in the men’s T47 100m final.According to sources, a heated argument broke out between Kedia and Satyanarayana over facilitating the athletes’ media interactions before they proceeded for mandatory dope-control procedures. The exchange allegedly escalated into a brief physical altercation before coaches and athletes stepped in to defuse the situation.The incident reportedly left several members of the para athletics contingent deeply upset, prompting the athletes, coaches and PCI officials to submit formal complaints to the sports ministry and the IOA seeking action.
Article Summary: Dilip Mahadu Gavit and Mohammed Basil Morssinganakathi have lodged formal complaints with the sports ministry and the Indian Olympic Association. They allege rude and disrespectful behaviour towards the country’s para athletes. The complaints name Sarvesh Kedia, an IOA media committee member.

Article Title: Shoulder surgery, 7 months out, one unforgettable throw: How Yash Vir Singh won CWG bronze
Article Text:
Yash Vir Singh

Before Glasgow glory came years of struggle

Yash Vir Singh (Special Arrangements)

The father who never gave up on Yash Vir

Yash Vir Singh with his father (Special Arrangements)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Before Yash Vir Singh walked up for his sixth and final throw in the men's javelin final at Scotstoun Stadium, two voices stayed with him.One came from Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra."You're throwing well. Just keep it straight and believe in yourself. It's your last throw, just make sure you don't foul. You can do it."The other came from his father and coach, Rai Singh."It's the last throw. Put everything into it."Seconds later, the javelin landed at 85.41 metres.Yash Vir leapt from seventh place to the bronze medal position, registering a personal best by almost three metres. The effort not only earned him a place on the podium alongside Neeraj Chopra, who took silver behind Sri Lanka's Rumesh Tharanga, but also made him only the third Indian to win a Commonwealth Games medal in men's javelin. For the first time in the history of the event, two Indians shared the Commonwealth Games podium.The medal came in one of the strongest men's javelin fields assembled at a Commonwealth Games.The Glasgow final featured one of the strongest javelin fields assembled at a Commonwealth Games. Besides Neeraj and Yash Vir, India also had Rohit Yadav in the final. Reigning Commonwealth Games champion Arshad Nadeem was back to defend his title.Former world champion Anderson Peters of Grenada, Trinidad and Tobago's Keshorn Walcott and former Commonwealth champion Julius Yego were all in the fray. Rumesh Tharanga, meanwhile, arrived in Glasgow after a series of impressive performances and eventually walked away with gold.For much of the evening, Yash Vir remained in the background.Having squeezed into the final in 10th place during qualification, few would have backed the Indian Railways ticket collector to leave Glasgow with a medal. His best throw heading into the final round measured 81.33m, leaving him seventh in the standings with one attempt remaining.Then came his final attempt."I'd made up my mind - today it was do or die. I shouted it out and then went for the throw. It wasn't easy. I'd already committed two fouls and even my fifth throw was only 76.95 metres. My only thought was to produce my personal best. I had nothing to lose. But there was a hunger built up over the last four years. I'll always remember that 85.41m throw. I'm immensely grateful to God," Yash Vir told TimesofIndia.com.The conditions hardly made life easier. Several leading throwers struggled to find consistency as gusty conditions made it difficult to judge the release. Yash Vir adjusted quickly."I quickly calculated the wind conditions. Then I increased my speed a bit and made a slight change to my technique according to the wind pressure. The plan was simple - release the javelin with full power. That's it. The plan worked. I'm happy that I finally crossed the 85-metre mark. My previous best was over 83 metres at the Inter State Championships."The bronze medal was the culmination of four years spent fighting through injury, surgery and rehabilitation, all while holding on to a promise he had made to himself."Main wapsi karke dikhaunga.[I'll make a comeback]."The promise was made in 2022.During a training session, Yash Vir injured his shoulder. The damage was serious. One of the muscles in his rotator cuff - the supraspinatus - had been affected, leaving him in constant pain and eventually requiring surgery at the Abhinav Bindra Targeting Performance (ABTP) Centre in Jaipur.The operation was successful, but it came with another challenge. Doctors ruled him out of competition for at least seven months. For an athlete whose life revolved around throwing the javelin, the rehabilitation was as much a mental battle as a physical one."It was an extremely difficult time. All I wanted was to return to the field," Yash Vir said."The surgery went well and my treatment was completed successfully. Dr Harshvardhan Singh and Dr Aditi Thakur are like God to me. They gave me the confidence that I would be able to throw the javelin again the way I always had. Today, I am here because of them. I owe them a lot."Unable to train, he spent months confined to bed. There was little he could do physically, so he tried to stay connected with the sport in every way possible. He watched videos of his old competitions, relived some of his best throws and immersed himself in motivational books, refusing to let the dream of competing again fade away.When he eventually returned in 2023, the signs were encouraging. His comeback competition ended with a silver medal. Strong performances followed over the next two seasons, eventually earning him a place in India's squad for the Commonwealth Games.Yet, despite steady progress, Yash Vir travelled to Glasgow with little fanfare.The spotlight naturally remained on Chopra, India's Olympic and world champion, while Rohit Yadav completed the three-member Indian contingent. Yash Vir entered the competition as an outsider, having qualified for the final in 10th place.Throughout the journey, one person remained at the centre of it all - his father, Rai Singh."Now, I don't want to look back. A Commonwealth Games medal means a lot to me. You can say this is just the beginning," he said.Behind that journey has been one constant figure. His father. Rai Singh is much more than Yash Vir's coach.A former national-level javelin thrower himself, Rai won multiple national medals and Railway championship titles before becoming an athletics coach with the Indian Railways. An NIS Diploma holder, he has guided his son's career from the very beginning, overseeing not just his technique but every aspect of his routine.Long before international medals entered the conversation, father and son spent countless hours training at the Railway Ground near Jaipur railway station.The first javelin wasn't even made of metal. It was bamboo."My father is very strict. He believes in discipline. He takes care of my training, schedule, diet and every single aspect of my life. I may be his son, but he is even stricter with me than anyone else," Yash Vir said."Whatever I am today is because of him. Foreign coaches come and go after a while, but it is my father who has taught me everything from the very beginning."Even now, the technical discussions happen at home."I don't know much about biomechanics. My father understands it really well. Whatever plan he gives me, whether it's about intensity, power, run-up or the release angle, everything comes from him."At Scotstoun Stadium, Rai Singh watched from above the runway, shouting instructions after every attempt. He had never received the opportunity to compete on one of athletics' biggest stages himself.On Saturday evening in Glasgow, he watched his son stand on the Commonwealth Games podium with a bronze medal around his neck. For Yash Vir, the medal represented a personal best, a national milestone and the fulfilment of a promise he had made to himself four years ago.
Article Summary: Yash Vir Singh wins bronze in the men's javelin at the Commonwealth Games. He is the third Indian to win a Commonwealth Games medal in the event. Sri Lanka's Rumesh Tharanga won gold and India's Neeraj Chopra took silver.

Article Title: Food poisoning denied me Commonwealth Games gold, says Selva Prabhu after winning bronze
Article Text:
India's Selva Prabhu Thirumaran competes in the men's triple jump final at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, Scotland.

Commonwealth Games bronze medallist Selva Prabhu believes food poisoning cost him a chance to win gold in Glasgow, saying a jump close to his personal best would have been enough to finish on top of the podium.Selva won bronze in the men's triple jump with a best effort of 16.52m, finishing behind fellow Indian Praveen Chithravel (16.58m) and Scotland's Jordon Scott (16.72m)."I wish I should have gotten that gold. I was really hoping for gold but what can be done when the competition begins, there is illness and food poisoning. I feel that in the end, there is always a cost to yourself. I am mentally tough so I decided, whatever happens, I will do it. Keep pushing myself," Selva told news agency PTI after returning from Glasgow on Monday.The Tamil Nadu athlete said the illness affected his performance and felt he missed a good opportunity, as a jump close to his personal best of 17.05m would have been enough to win the event."I should have stayed healthy, but it's for the next time I'm always ready. I can compete more, stay healthy. It's about the stage. I have the consistency.It's all about that particular day. I just always want to stay healthy. Now, I want to work on my approach. Once I get the hang of it, I can do it," he said.When asked about the upcoming Asian Games, Selva said his focus remains on taking one step at a time."I live each day. Each day requires a new performance. You just cannot target a gold like that. Yes, I am now looking forward to qualifying for the Asian Games first and then taking it from there," he said.The Athletics Federation of India (AFI) is yet to announce the Indian team for the Asian Games in Japan.
Article Summary: Selva Prabhu believes food poisoning cost him a chance to win gold in Glasgow. Tamil Nadu athlete says a jump close to his personal best of 17.05m would have been enough to win. Selva won bronze in the men's triple jump with a best effort of 16.52m.

Article Title: CWG 2026: Glasgow restaurant deletes Instagram account after Lovlina Borgohain flags 'incorrect map' of India
Article Text:
Lovlina Borgohain (AP Photo)

Lovlina says she felt hurt

Restaurant issues apology

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

BFI chief says there was no confrontation

NEW DELHI: A Glasgow-based Indian restaurant deleted its Instagram account after Olympic medallist Lovlina Borgohain pointed out that its logo and napkins showed an incorrect map of India.The incident happened after the Indian boxing team visited Mister Singh's India - The Home of Curry to celebrate its historic Commonwealth Games 2026 campaign. India finished with a record 10 boxing medals - seven gold and three silver.During the dinner, Lovlina noticed that the map printed on the restaurant's napkins and displayed outside the restaurant did not include India's Northeast.A video of her raising the issue went viral on social media and drew criticism from many users.Lovlina, who is from Assam and won a silver medal in Glasgow, politely raised the issue with the restaurant management."Please don't take this the wrong way. I felt a little hurt by this. In the map of India, our North East is missing. Yes, even outside, the map that's displayed has cut off the North East. As someone from the North East, that really hurts us. That's all I wanted to say. Please keep this in mind next time. Thank you so much."Soon after the video surfaced, the restaurant issued a public apology and accepted its mistake. It also said the logo would be changed."Mr Singh's India, is very proud of our Indian heritage and ancestry, for almost 32 years we have served, for India and around the world.""First and foremost, we would like to unequivocally apologise for the depiction of the wrong map of India. We will take immediate steps to correct this. Once again our sincere apologies, we never wanted to offend anyone rather wanted to serve with pride to Indian contingent."The restaurant also thanked the Indian team for visiting after their successful campaign."We will change the logo with proper map. It was our humble privilege and honour, that we served team India, after their fantastic, achievements in the Commonwealth Games. All athletes and guests thoroughly enjoyed their evening, these memories will last with us for India. Team Mr Singh India."Shortly after issuing the apology, the restaurant's Instagram account was deleted.Boxing Federation of India president Ajay Singh, who was present at the restaurant, said the matter was handled peacefully."There was no confrontation. It was an aberration and we pointed that out, me and Lovlina. They accepted their mistake and assured us that it will be corrected," Singh told PTI.The restaurant has hosted several visiting sports teams and dignitaries over the years.
Article Summary: Olympic medallist Lovlina Borgohain points out that restaurant's logo and napkins showed an incorrect map of India. Incident happened after Indian boxing team visited Mister Singh's India - The Home of Curry to celebrate its historic Commonwealth Games 2026 campaign.

Jadumani Singh (55kg) and Asian Games bronze medallist Narender Berwal (+90kg) settled for silver.India's previous best boxing performance at the Commonwealth Games came in Gold Coast in 2018, when the team won seven medals, including three gold.India also enjoyed its best-ever Commonwealth Games in judo.Unnati Sharma added a bronze medal in the women's 63kg event after defeating South Africa's Skye Knoester by ippon in just one minute and seven seconds in the bronze-medal contest.She had lost to Australia's Saya Middleton in the semifinal but bounced back to finish on the podium.The bronze took India's judo medal tally to four, the country's best at the Commonwealth Games.Harsh Singh (men's -60kg) and Asmita Dey (women's -48kg) created history by becoming India's first-ever Commonwealth Games judo gold medallists. Yamini Mourya won silver in the women's -57kg category.Harsh Tokas narrowly missed a bronze medal in the men's -81kg event after losing to Australia's Keishin Ochi by ippon. He took bronze in the event after earlier winning silver in the men's 10,000m, making him the first Indian track and field athlete to win two individual medals at a single Commonwealth Games.India also celebrated a double podium finish in the men's triple jump. Praveen Chithravel won silver with 16.58m, while Selva Prabhu Thirumaran claimed bronze with 16.52m.Ramesh Shanmugam finished seventh in the men's T54 1500m para final. Priyanka Goswami finished seventh in the women's 10,000m race walk with a season-best time of 45:53.93, while Ravina was disqualified.In the men's pole vault, Dev Kumar Meena finished fourth with 5.30m and Kuldeep Kumar placed sixth with 5.10m.India's para athletes enjoyed their best-ever Commonwealth Games.The 28-member para contingent finished with seven medals - three gold, two silver and two bronze - matching the total number of medals India had won across all previous Commonwealth Games editions.Para track and field athletes won six medals - three gold, two silver and one bronze - while Jhandu Kumar added a bronze medal in para powerlifting.

Late heroics rescue TS Galaxy

TS Galaxy's Sipho Maseti leaves fans stunned after handling the ball outside the area in stoppage time, apparently fooled by the extra markings on a dual-purpose pitchTS Galaxy goalkeeper Sipho Maseti produced one of the most bizarre moments of the new South African Premiership season after appearing to mistake a rugby field marking for the edge of his penalty area, earning a straight red card in a dramatic stoppage-time incident.The unusual dismissal came during TS Galaxy's 2-2 draw against Siwelele FC at Dr. Petrus Molemela Stadium, with video of the incident quickly going viral and leaving football fans around the world stunned.With the match deep into added time and the scores locked at 2-2, Maseti comfortably moved forward to collect a long clearance. Believing he was still inside his penalty area, the goalkeeper picked up the ball with his hands — only to realise moments later that he had crossed outside the 18-yard box.The referee immediately produced a straight red card for deliberate handball outside the area, while Maseti stood in disbelief after his costly misjudgment.The incident is believed to have been caused by the extra markings on the dual-purpose surface at Dr. Petrus Molemela Stadium, which also hosts rugby matches.Replays appeared to show Maseti confusing one of the rugby field lines with the boundary of his own penalty area, prompting him to handle the ball several metres outside the legal zone.The sending-off capped a forgettable outing for the TS Galaxy goalkeeper, who had earlier gifted Siwelele their opening goal when his attempted clearance ricocheted off forward Siphesihle Jeza and into the net.Despite those setbacks, TS Galaxy battled back through a Victor Letsoalo penalty and a Veluyeke Zulu header to keep themselves in the contest.Maseti's red card threatened to undo all of Galaxy's hard work, but the visitors found an unlikely hero in substitute goalkeeper Ira Tape.Thrown into action immediately after the dismissal, Tape produced an outstanding save from Jordan Marks' resulting free-kick to preserve the 2-2 draw and ensure TS Galaxy escaped with a valuable point.While Maseti's dismissal became one of the defining moments of the opening weekend, the dramatic finish also highlighted Galaxy's resilience after twice recovering from setbacks.
Article Summary: TS Galaxy goalkeeper Sipho Maseti sent off during 2-2 draw against Siwelele FC. Maseto appeared to mistake rugby field marking for the edge of his penalty area. Video of the incident quickly went viral and left football fans stunned.

Article Title: 'Shutdown a board decision, will honour players' contracts': Tata Steel on Jamshedpur FC shutdown
Article Text:
Jamshedpur FC players (Pic credit: Jamshedpur FC)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

KOLKATA: Even as an online petition was started by fans all over the country to save Jamshedpur FC and appeals to save the club kept growing louder, Tata Steel vice-president clarified in a news conference in Jamshedpur on Monday that the decision was entirely that of the Tata Steel board and the company will fulfil the players’ current contracts.“The decision is entirely Tata Steel board’s and has no connection of any kind with any financial irregularity or discrepancy,” Tata Steel vice-president (corporate services), DB Sundar Ramam said.“Players will receive full payment as per their contract. Besides this, Tata Steel will also try to ensure that these players can get opportunities to play in other clubs, so that their careers are not adversely affected in any way.”Sundar Ramam said the aim of the company was never to earn profit in sports but to “provide opportunities to players, promote sports culture and prepare future talent” and that was the philosophy with which it operated Jamshedpur FC over the years.“Tata Steel invested about Rs 30 to 35 crore annually in the club’s operations, and, with the support of other sponsors, about Rs 320 crore has been invested in the club so far.In the last 9 years, JFC made many accomplishments and Tata Steel is proud of this entire journey,” he added.He also added that the aim of the company will remain on grassroots development.“The closure of JFC’s operations does not mean that football will end in Jamshedpur. Tata Steel will continue to provide every possible support in the city for football competitions, local clubs, training programmes and young players,” he said while adding that Jamshedpur’s rich football tradition will continue and new talents will keep getting opportunities to move forward.
Article Summary: Tata Steel vice-president DB Sundar Ramam said the decision was entirely that of the Tata Steel board and the company will fulfil the players’ current contracts. He added that the company was never to earn profit in sports but to “provide opportunities to players, promote sports culture and prepare future talent”

Article Title: Durand Cup: Doley hat-trick keeps Raengdai's fairytale alive as debutants edge TRAU in seven-goal Manipur derby
Article Text:
FC Raengdai players celebrate. (Pic Credit: Durand Cup Media)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

There seems to be no stopping FC Raengdai! After making a historic winning debut in Durand Cup, the newest football sensation from Manipur continued their run, this time with a thrilling 4-3 win over TRAU FC in a much-anticipated Manipur derby on Monday.Before the packed crowd at Khuman Lampak Main Stadium in Imphal, Mridul Doley headed in a corner kick in the 79th minute to complete his hat-trick and help Raengdai edge TRAU and stay on their fairytale journey in football.The win took the debutants to top of Group D with six points from two matches, a start few would have predicted a week earlier. NEROCA sit second on one point from a single outing, with TRAU third, also on one point but in two games. Indian Navy occupy the fourth spot without a win to their name.Reangdai attacker Doley, who had provided the assist in the solitary goal that won them the game against Indian Navy, was the star from early on, scoring on either side of the half-hour to give Raengdai a comfortable lead.TRAU’s response arrived just before the interval through Chanam Akash Meitei, only for Chongtham Kishan Singh to restore the two-goal lead in first-half stoppage time.Afdal Varikkodan pulled one back within two minutes of the restart, and when Lanchungrei Pamei turned the ball into his own net in the 67th minute, parity had been restored for the second time on the day.However, Doley had the final word, completing a memorable hat-trick to send Raengdai in lead again, this time till the final whistle.Earlier, FC1 marked their Durand Cup debut with a spirited 2-1 comeback victory over Karbi Anglong Morning Star FC in a Group F fixture at Indira Gandhi Athletic Stadium in Guwahati on Monday.Meanwhile, another debutants Langsning FC produced a sensational second-half display to cruise to a commanding 5-0 victory over Mumbay FC in a Group E fixture at the Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium in Shillong on the day.
Article Summary: FC Raengdai beat TRAU FC 4-3 in a much-anticipated Manipur derby on Monday. Mridul Doley scored a hat-trick to help the debutants top Group D. Earlier, FC1 marked their Durand Cup debut with a spirited 2-1 comeback victory over Karbi Anglong Morning Star FC.

Article Title: Brazil game can't mask Indian football's crisis: Bhutia says 'timing of the match is a problem'
Article Text:
Bhaichung Bhutia (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The announcement of a glamour friendly between India and Brazil should have been a moment of celebration for Indian football. Instead, it has exposed the widening gap between spectacle and substance, prompting former India captain Bhaichung Bhutia to question both the timing and the purpose of the high-profile fixture.“The timing of the Brazil friendly is a problem for me,” Bhutia said, pointing out that India will be involved in the FIFA ASEAN Cup around the same period. “The FIFA ASEAN Cup will be taking place at that time and we don’t know how the national team will be formed.” His concerns are difficult to dismiss. India, ranked 138th in the world, have been drawn alongside Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore in the ASEAN Cup, a tournament where only the group winner advances.With qualification already a challenging prospect, diverting attention towards an exhibition match raises legitimate questions about priorities. Bhutia’s criticism goes beyond scheduling. For him, the Brazil match has become a symbol of a football ecosystem struggling to address its fundamental problems.“I was wondering about the purpose of the friendly match against Brazil. Is Indian football going to gain anything out of it?” he asked.The question strikes at the heart of the debate. A match against five-time world champions Brazil will undoubtedly generate excitement, television audiences and commercial interest. But can a single evening against one of football’s global giants compensate for years of structural decline? The former captain believes it cannot. “A big corporate group like the Tatas have declared shutting down of Jamshedpur FC. It goes to show the health of Indian football,” he said.The uncertainty surrounding Jamshedpur FC has only amplified concerns about the financial sustainability of Indian football. At a time when clubs are struggling, developmental pathways remain weak and investment is shrinking, a marquee international fixture risks appearing disconnected from the realities on the ground.Bhutia painted an even bleaker picture of the current state of the game. “The focus of the football federation should be getting the house in order. Let alone the seniors, even the U-17s are failing to earn qualification in continental tournaments,” he said. “The national league is in disarray, the junior programme is rudderless and there is no money to develop the grassroots game.”His views have found support within the playing community. India full-back Nikhil Poojary echoed similar concerns on social media, noting the contrast between celebrating Brazil’s visit and waking up to news of another club shutting down operations.India has hosted football royalty before. Uruguay and Argentina played in the Nehru Cup during the 1980s, while Lionel Messi’s Argentina visited in 2011 and again in 2025. Those occasions generated excitement and memories, but they did little to alter the trajectory of Indian football.
Article Summary: Bhaichung Bhutia questions the purpose of India's friendly against Brazil. Former India captain also questions the timing of the fixture. India will also be taking part in the FIFA ASEAN Cup at the same time. BhUTia believes the Brazil match is a symbol of Indian football's problems.

Article Title: Harshita Jakhar scripts history, becomes first Indian woman ever at Tour de France Femmes
Article Text:
India's Harshita Jakhar poses with UCI President David Lappartient ()

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Harshita eyes bigger goals



Indian cyclist Harshita Jakhar created history by becoming the first Indian woman to be part of the Tour de France Femmes.The 19-year-old rode alongside seven other young cyclists from Afghanistan, Algeria, Chile, Ethiopia, Namibia and Uganda during the ceremonial start of Stage 2 on Sunday.The group, selected by the Union Cycliste Internationale (UCI), completed a 4.5-km neutralised section of the course before the professional riders began the stage. The Tour de France Femmes, which runs from August 1 to 9, is the women's version of the famous Tour de France and is part of the UCI Women's World Tour.UCI President David Lappartient welcomed the riders before the stage and praised Harshita's achievement.“We are excited to have India's very talented Harshita Jakhar in our prestigious UCI World Cycling Talent programme. I am sure she will love being part of the Tour de France Femmes and will soon return to take part in the actual competition,” he said.Harshita, who hails from Rajasthan, said riding at the Tour de France Femmes was a dream come true."Ever since I fell in love with cycling as a child, thanks to my father, I have dreamt of the Tour de France.I am thankful to UCI for giving me this opportunity to ride with other talented cyclists at the start of the Second Stage of the race for women," Harshita said.A rising star in Indian cycling, Harshita has won several junior titles and is now competing successfully at the senior level. She trains at the SAI National Centre of Excellence in Patiala under the guidance of her father, former Commonwealth Games cyclist Rakesh Jakhar. Her long-term goals are a top-10 finish at the 2026 Asian Games and a medal at the 2030 edition.
Article Summary: Harshita Jakhar is the first Indian woman to be part of the Tour de France Femmes. The 19-year-old rode alongside seven other young cyclists from Afghanistan, Algeria, Chile, Ethiopia, Namibia and Uganda. Harshita's long-term goals are a top-10 finish at the 2026 Asian Games and a medal at the 2030 edition.

Article Title: OFFSIDE | Gianni Infantino: The man who tried to sell football
Article Text:
How FIFA’s most powerful president tried to turn football’s greatest prize into a $20-billion investment vehicle — and finally discovered the limits of his power.

Infantino says ‘nobody’ is trying to sell the World Cup. (AI Cartoon by Nirmalya Dutta.)

The Trojan Horse

bandobast

bandobast

Infantino’s Trojan horse of privatisation fell flat. (AI cartoon by Nirmalya Dutta)

The fallout

The end of the road?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Hello and welcome to a new version of OFFSIDE, a weekly newsletter looking at everything happening in the Beautiful Game.One pivotal moment in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey shows just how far the film departs from Homer’s epic. In the original, Odysseus tells the Cyclops Polyphemus that his name is “Outis”, meaning “Nobody” or “No One”, before he and his men blind him. When the other Cyclopes come to check on Polyphemus, they are told that “Nobody” is attacking him, leaving them with little reason to intervene.Odysseus escapes the cave, yet cannot resist taunting Polyphemus and revealing his true identity. That gives the Cyclops everything he needs to escalate the complaint to his father, Poseidon, god of the sea, who turns the journey home for Odysseus and Co into the ancient Ryanair experience. That version doesn’t exist in Nolan’s movie, which transforms Odysseus from Homer’s polytropos, the “man of many turns” whose cunning is matched by the hubris that angers the gods, into a traumatised veteran who simply wants to return home to his wife.Speaking of hubris that angers the gods, Gianni Infantino, a man who has changed football in every feasible way to improve FIFA’s relationship with Mammon, was at it again after his plan to “sell the World Cup” was leaked.Once caught out, he channelled his inner Odysseus and insisted that “nobody” was selling football.The comparison ends there.Odysseus’ Trojan Horse made it through the gates of Troy. Infantino’s never got past the turnstile, perhaps because this was hardly his first rodeo and, for once, the footballing world decided, to borrow a line from Sir Alex Ferguson, to check under the pasta to see what was under the sauce.So here’s the Homeric story of the modern-day Odysseus, who thought he could get away with it all till the footballing world finally caught on.Much as it describes Homer’s protagonist, the word– a man of many turns – could very well be used to describe the Swiss man from a nondescript village who had become the most powerful man in football’s history, one whom Donald Trump referred to as the “King of Soccer”. Perhaps he felt even the Fates were intervening on his behalf when the winds blew Donald Trump back into the White House to ensure that the FIFA World Cup in America would be everything his heart desired.One particular anecdote illustrates how Infantino came to view himself amid the pantheon of global soccer stars and movers and shakers in international politics.In India, there’s a term calledthat translates to “arrangement”, “management” or “organisation”. It refers to the deployment of police, security protocols and logistical arrangements when a VIP is in town and is seen by many as a social marker of power. According to a report by Martyn Ziegler in The Sunday Times, FIFA requested a similarfor him in Canada, seeking the same transport privileges reserved for the US president. The request was declined by Canadian police.Therequest was just the tip of the iceberg. Infantino even has a personal photographer as his “Instagram husband”, someone whose job is to click every moment of his life. He engraved his name twice on the Club World Cup trophy and cast himself as a global peacemaker who brought two “warring nations” to the World Cup.All that is evident in the handprint he has left on the global game.During his tenure, Infantino has managed to expand the World Cup from 32 teams to 48 teams, revamped the Club World Cup into a mini-World Cup with 32 teams, broken football’s long-standing traditions to force through hydration breaks and a half-time show, introduced dynamic pricing for FIFA matches and got players’ bans rescinded, including Ronaldo’s and Folarin Balogun’s. He gave Trump a FIFA Peace Prize when the Nobel Committee wouldn’t give him one and engineered the 2030 tournament by ensuring that it would be played across Europe, Africa and South America to ensure that Saudi Arabia got it in 2034.Earlier, he also tried to push through a secretive $25-billion, 12-year proposal involving SoftBank that envisaged an expanded Club World Cup and a global Nations League culminating in a “Final 8” tournament. That fell through, and he even tried to hold the World Cup every two years instead of four.While neither went forward, both moves emboldened Infantino to think that perhaps his FFE Trojan Horse would go through unchecked.The FFE plan, which sounds rather innocuous, like corporate CSR efforts, was very simple: create a different entity called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), a subsidiary dealing with FIFA’s main mission: improving its relationship with the only god that matters, Mammon.The new company would take care of everything financial: broadcasting rights, sponsorship, ticketing and operational delivery. JPMorgan valued this company at $20 billion, and FIFA would sell a $4.2-billion stake to outside investors while retaining 80%. The pitch was that FIFA was “undermonetised”, with annual revenue of $3.6 billion compared with the NFL’s $21.2 billion, MLB’s $13.1 billion and the NBA’s $12.5 billion.The idea was to grow FIFA’s event portfolio, a hard ask given that the NFL and others are annual franchise leagues, while FIFA is a governing body whose main income is concentrated around periodic tournaments. Infantino hoped to pull this off by promising FIFA’s 211 members $20 million during the next four-year cycle, double the $10 million they were due to receive, with one caveat: they had to come on board as soon as possible.Infantino envisaged himself as the chair of this company once he retired from FIFA in 2030, with a basic annual salary of $30 million, even joking that by 2031 “we can make serious money”. When asked whether his current $6 million annual salary wasn’t enough, he replied: “No, I’m talking a serious amount.”For Odysseus, the fallout started when he announced his name to the Cyclops Polyphemus, earning Poseidon’s wrath. For Infantino, the fallout began on July 28, when The Times (UK) and the Financial Times, in a moment reminiscent of Leibniz and Newton’s independent development of calculus, laid bare Infantino’s plan to sell stakes to a private company. The proposed investor group would be led by Josh Kushner, brother of Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law. FIFA was at pains to point out that Josh, unlike his brother, was a registered Democrat who had donated to Obama’s campaign and attended Taylor Swift’s wedding. According to Forbes, he has a net worth of $5.2 billion. In the finance world in particular, Josh is the one who matters and is known for his financial acumen, including a major investment in Instagram that doubled in value in a few days.The angriest remonstrations – enough to make Gertrude wonder whether UEFA “doth protest too much” – came from Europe, which said the “soul and governance of football are not assets to be sold”, a worldview seldom expressed when teams of sportswashing nations break UEFA’s financial fair play regulations.Things came to a head when all 55 UEFA nations agreed to boycott the men’s and women’s World Cups. CONCACAF opposed FFE over the lack of due process, while the AFC called the plan “totally unacceptable”.Senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro resigned, calling it a “bad deal for football”, while FIFA’s chief operating officer (COO), Kevin Lamour, claimed that they had been “deceived” and that it was the “project of one person”.Soon, the screws started turning for Infantino, with UEFA saying FIFA’s leadership had lost “UEFA’s confidence”. CONCACAF said the plan was a “symptom of leadership that has stopped putting football first”. The English FA said it would send a letter to Infantino withdrawing its support for his re-election. Other European nations are expected to follow suit. In fact, UEFA has the power to trigger an Extraordinary FIFA Congress without help from any other confederation. The rules require 20% of FIFA’s 211 members, or 43 associations, and UEFA has 55. Calls for his resignation are also gaining traction. UK PM Andy Burnham, freshly burnished in the role after Starmer’s resignation, has called for him to step down. LaLiga president Javier Tebas has followed suit.Of course, Infantino retains strong support from CAF, CONMEBOL and smaller Asian, Caribbean and Pacific federations that rely heavily on FIFA’s development funding.Perhaps Infantino’s time is up and his fate seems sealed, like that of a tragic hero from the Russian rather than the Greek tradition. The alacrity with which folks who benefited from Infantino turning football into a capitalist behemoth have suddenly discovered hitherto unseen principles is very reminiscent of an old Russian short story by Anton Chekhov titled The Confession. Its protagonist is a cashier who suddenly becomes the cat that got the cream when he gets a minor promotion and finds himself courted, respected and invited by everyone.Then, as he gets mired in scandal, he is quickly dropped. The patrons disappear, and his family turns scornful. The court is only loyal as long as the gifts keep coming; as soon as the gifts become liabilities, that loyalty develops a conscience.Infantino hasn’t been banished from Zurich yet, but he is getting the treatment that would have befallen Odysseus if the Trojan Horse had been burned instead of taken inside the walled city. For the last decade, Infantino has been treated as soccer’s God, but over the past few extraordinary days, he has come to be treated as the man who tarnished world football, even as everyone enjoys the fruits of his spoils. One wouldn’t be surprised if Infantino suddenly felt like quoting Chekhov’s cashier: “My dear ladies and gentlemen, I got caught, or to state it more fully: yesterday I was respected and honoured on all sides; today I am a scoundrel and a thief. .. Cry out, now, banish me, write editorials, and throw stones, please—not everyone.”
Article Summary: Gianni Infantino tried to turn the World Cup into a $20-billion investment vehicle. The FIFA president has become the most powerful man in football’s history. He has changed football in every feasible way to improve FIFA's relationship with Mammon. FIFA has also introduced a half-time pricing dynamic, breaking long-standing traditions.

Article Title: World Cup rights gamble backfires: Wales withdraw support for Infantino's FIFA re-election bid
Article Text:
Gianni Infantino

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Wales have become the first home nation to withdraw support for Gianni Infantino's bid to remain FIFA president after his proposal to sell a stake in the commercial rights of the World Cup and other FIFA competitions was abandoned.The Football Association of Wales (FAW) said it will no longer back Infantino's re-election campaign for the 2027-2031 term, following concerns over the failed investment plan.FIFA had proposed raising up to $4.2 billion by selling about a 20% stake in a new entity that would manage the commercial rights of competitions including the World Cup. However, the proposal was withdrawn on Friday after facing strong opposition from stakeholders.With the plan shelved, attention has shifted to the possible impact on Infantino's chances of securing another term as FIFA president.The proposal had also triggered strong criticism from across world football. UEFA had warned it could boycott FIFA competitions, including the World Cup, if the plan went ahead.On Saturday, both UEFA and Concacaf, the governing body for football in North, Central America and the Caribbean, issued statements criticising FIFA's leadership following Infantino's decision to withdraw the proposal.The FAW is among the first national football associations to publicly oppose Infantino's re-election.In a statement, the FAW confirmed "its withdrawal of support for the candidature of Gianni Infantino for re-election as Fifa president for the 2027-2031 term".Explaining its decision, the Welsh governing body said:"The recent failures in good governance, processes, leadership, values, stakeholder management, communications and sound judgement have led us to a position where Mr Infantino has lost the confidence of the FAW to remain at the helm of world football."Failing to put the best interests of football first is a failure we cannot accept."
Article Summary: Wales withdraw support for Gianni Infantino's bid to remain FIFA president. Football Association of Wales said it will no longer back his re-election campaign. FIFA had proposed raising up to $4.2 billion by selling a 20% stake in a new entity.

Article Title: 'Vozinha! Vozinha!': FIFA World Cup breakout star gets hero's welcome in Chile after three delays
Article Text:
Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha arrives at the airport ahead of a move to Colo-Colo in Santiago, Chile. (AP Photo)

Three delays before dream move finally became reality



World Cup hero earns special jersey exception



Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

One of the biggest breakout stars of the 2026 FIFA World Cup has finally arrived in Chile — and the reception was nothing short of extraordinary.Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha, whose remarkable performances at the World Cup captured the imagination of football fans across the globe, landed in Santiago on Sunday to complete his move to Chilean giants Colo Colo after his arrival was delayed on three separate occasions.Hundreds of jubilant supporters gathered at Santiago's airport with flags, banners, drums and chants, turning the veteran goalkeeper's arrival into a celebration usually reserved for legends. Videos of the emotional welcome quickly spread across social media, underlining the popularity Vozinha has earned since his unforgettable World Cup campaign."I’m very happy to be here. And I want to thank the fans for the patience they’ve shown while waiting for me," the 40-year-old told reporters shortly after landing. "See you at the Monumental Stadium."Colo Colo, Chile's most successful football club, announced the signing of Josimar Évora Dias — better known worldwide as Vozinha — on July 24.However, what was expected to be a straightforward transfer soon became a complicated saga.Documentation issues and personal matters delayed the goalkeeper's arrival three different times, raising concerns among supporters eagerly waiting to welcome their new signing.The uncertainty finally ended on Sunday evening when Vozinha landed in Santiago at 8:35 p.m. local time to a rousing reception from hundreds of Colo Colo fans.The veteran is scheduled to undergo medical examinations before signing an initial six-month contract with an option to extend it by another year. He is expected to begin training with his new teammates on Tuesday before being officially unveiled by the club.Vozinha's move has already prompted an unprecedented rule change in Chilean football.The Chilean Football Federation unanimously voted to amend its regulations and allow the goalkeeper to wear "Vozinha" on the back of his jersey instead of his surname.Under previous league rules, players were required to display only their family names on their shirts.The exception reflects the global recognition attached to the nickname that became synonymous with Cape Verde's historic World Cup journey.Vozinha — whose nickname means "grandma" in Portuguese — became one of the tournament's most celebrated players after helping Cape Verde make history on their World Cup debut.At 40, he became the oldest player to feature in a nation's first-ever World Cup match and earned worldwide admiration with a string of spectacular saves against Spain, Uruguay and Argentina. His heroic display against eventual champions Spain, where he kept them scoreless, transformed him into one of the faces of the tournament.His popularity exploded during the competition. Before the World Cup, Vozinha had fewer than 50,000 Instagram followers. By the end of the tournament, that figure had soared beyond 29.5 million.For Colo Colo supporters, the excitement extends well beyond social media fame.Fans hope the experienced goalkeeper can inspire the Chilean league leaders to another domestic title before leading their challenge in next season's Copa Libertadores.
Article Summary: Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha lands in Chile to complete move to Colo Colo. The 40-year-old became one of the biggest breakout stars of the 2026 FIFA World Cup. His arrival at Santiago's airport was met by hundreds of jubilant fans.
